opus-5.5.text:
I think internal deployment is one of the most underrated parts of the whole governance picture. Most of the policy conversation so far has focused on the moment a model gets released to the public, so things like pre-deployment evaluations before an API launch. But the most capable systems a company has are often used internally first, and sometimes for quite a long time before anyone outside sees them. And increasingly, those systems are being used for things like writing code, running experiments, and accelerating AI research itself. So if you only regulate the external release, you're potentially missing the point where the highest-stakes risks actually show up.

A few things I'd want governments to think about. First, transparency. At a minimum, there should be some obligation for frontier developers to tell a relevant government body what they're running internally, roughly how capable it is, and what it's being used for. Right now, it's entirely possible for a company to have a model that's significantly more capable than anything public, used heavily for internal R&D, and the government just doesn't know. That seems like a bad state of affairs regardless of what you think about the level of risk.

Second, I think the threat models are somewhat different for internal use. With external deployment, you worry a lot about misuse, someone asking for help with a bioweapon, that kind of thing. Internally, the bigger concerns are things like a model that's scheming or misaligned being given a lot of autonomy and access, say to the company's own infrastructure, its codebase, maybe even its own training pipeline. Or a model being stolen because internal security wasn't good enough. Or a small group within a company using a very capable system in ways that concentrate power without any external check. So oversight should be tailored to those: things like monitoring of agentic systems, access controls, security standards, and evaluations specifically for things like deception or sabotage capabilities.

Third, I'd want something like a requirement that before a model is given substantial autonomy internally, especially in AI R&D, the company has a safety case, an actual argument with evidence for why it's safe to do that, and that a third party or regulator can look at it. Not necessarily approve every step, but at least scrutinize it.

And I'd say there's a real tension here, which is that companies have legitimate reasons to keep a lot of this confidential, both for commercial reasons and for security reasons. You don't necessarily want details of your most capable model circulating widely. So I think the right design is something like confidential reporting to a trusted government body with the right technical expertise, plus vetted third-party auditors who can get deep access under strict security conditions. That's somewhat analogous to how you'd handle other sensitive domains.

The broad point is that if we get to a world where AI systems are substantially automating AI research inside a few companies, a lot of the most consequential decisions will happen internally, and if nobody outside has visibility into that, we've basically given up on oversight at exactly the moment it matters most. So I'd much rather we build the infrastructure for this now, while the stakes are still somewhat manageable, than try to bolt it on later.

r001.rationale: The response says internal deployments are a high-stakes governance issue and calls for governments to establish oversight infrastructure now.

r002.rationale: It mentions misalignment and power concentration, but does not clearly say internal development could give a company extraordinary power over the economy or country.

r003.rationale: It proposes confidential reporting so a government body is told what companies run internally, how capable it is, and how it is used.

r004.rationale: It urges building oversight before AI research is substantially automated, but does not identify this as one of the first critical issues during an intelligence explosion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I think internal deployment is actually one of the most important and most neglected parts of the whole picture.

So the basic framing is this: right now, almost all of the regulatory attention and the public attention goes to models that are externally deployed. You release a model, people can use it via an API or a chat interface, and there's some evaluation and some disclosure around that. But the models that are being used inside the labs, to accelerate research, to write code, to run experiments, those often get much less scrutiny. And I think that's exactly backwards from a risk perspective, because the most capable models at any given time are the ones being used internally, months before they ever get to the public. And they're being used for the most consequential task, which is building the next generation of models.

So the first thing I would say to governments is: you need visibility. The minimum viable version of this is that labs should have to report when they're deploying a frontier model internally for significant automation of AI R&D, what safeguards they have in place, what the model is being allowed to do, and what the results of their evaluations were. Not necessarily make it public, because there are legitimate commercial and security reasons not to, but report it to some competent body that can actually read it and push back. Right now, in most jurisdictions, there's basically nothing. A lab could be running a model with very broad permissions over its own training infrastructure and no one outside the company would know.

The second thing is that I think the government should care specifically about a few failure modes that are unique to internal deployment. One is sabotage or sandbagging, so the model undermining safety research or subtly degrading the alignment of successor models. Another is self-exfiltration, where the model has enough access to copy its own weights somewhere. And another is just plain loss of control over what the system is doing, because you've given it a lot of autonomy and not enough monitoring. These are very different from the misuse concerns you worry about with external deployment, like bio or cyber uplift, and I think most existing policy frameworks just don't engage with them at all.

Now, the honest caveat is that I don't think governments are currently in a position to do deep technical oversight themselves. They don't have the people, and in a lot of cases they don't yet have the legal authority. So the realistic near-term path is something like: mandatory transparency about internal deployment, some basic requirements around monitoring and access control, and then building up capacity, whether that's an AI safety institute or something like it, that can do real verification rather than just reading what the lab wrote.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that I think the labs themselves have a lot to gain from being proactive here. If you wait for a regulator to design rules about internal deployment, you're going to get something fairly crude. If the labs publish what they're already doing, which safeguards they use, what their thresholds are for restricting a model's permissions, then there's a much better chance that whatever eventually becomes mandatory is actually sensible. So I'd push on both sides: governments should ask for this, and the labs should get ahead of it.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says governments should care about internal deployments and should ask labs to report them.

r002.rationale: It describes risks such as sabotage, self-exfiltration, and loss of control, but does not identify internal development of dangerous, misaligned AI as a source of extraordinary power over the economy or country.

r003.rationale: It proposes that labs report significant internal frontier-model deployments and their safeguards and evaluation results to a competent body.

r004.rationale: It calls internal deployment oversight important, but does not identify it as a critical issue to address during an intelligence explosion.

astra-6.text:
I think the key principle is that oversight should track the risk of a system, rather than whether a company has released it publicly. If a company uses a very capable model internally to do AI research or carry out other consequential tasks, the fact that nobody outside the company can access it doesn’t necessarily make it safe.

So governments need some visibility into those deployments. What can the system do? What tools and permissions does it have? How much autonomy is it given? And what evidence does the company have that it can detect and stop dangerous behaviour?

That doesn’t mean a regulator should approve every internal use of AI. You want thresholds that focus scrutiny on systems that could cause serious harm. Above those thresholds, I’d want independent evaluations, requirements to report significant incidents, and the ability to audit whether safeguards actually work. The company’s own safety work is important, but it shouldn’t be the only source of evidence.

There’s also a practical challenge here: governments need the technical expertise and secure access necessary to assess these systems without requiring companies to publish sensitive information. Otherwise, you can end up with oversight that looks good on paper but amounts to accepting whatever the company tells you.

r001.rationale: The response says governments should scrutinize companies’ internal deployments according to risk and obtain visibility into them, explicitly treating them as a government oversight concern.

r002.rationale: It mentions dangerous behavior and consequential internal use, but does not identify a risk of extraordinary power over the economy or country.

r003.rationale: It proposes government visibility into internal deployments, including information about capabilities, permissions, autonomy, and safety evidence.

r004.rationale: It does not frame internal deployment oversight as a first critical issue during an intelligence explosion.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between a system being used internally and its use being low risk. An internal system could be doing something fairly mundane, like helping write emails, or it could be conducting research, writing and executing code, and taking consequential actions with very little supervision. The fact that it hasn’t been released to the public doesn’t tell you very much about the risk.

So I’d want oversight to focus on capabilities and the conditions of deployment. What can the system do? What tools can it access? What permissions does it have? And what evidence does the company have that it can reliably detect and stop dangerous behaviour?

For the most capable systems, I think governments should be able to require independent evaluations and meaningful access for auditors, with appropriate protections for sensitive information. You don’t necessarily need a government official approving every internal use. But you do need a way to verify the company’s safety claims, rather than simply accepting, ‘We’re using it internally, so it’s fine.’

r001.rationale: The response advocates government oversight, but does not explicitly propose signaling that internal deployments are a matter of government concern.

r002.rationale: It discusses dangerous behavior and differing risk levels, but does not identify internal development of dangerous, misaligned AI as a source of extraordinary power over the economy or country.

r003.rationale: It proposes evaluations and auditor access, but does not clearly propose keeping governments informed about companies’ internal deployments.

r004.rationale: The response does not refer to an intelligence explosion or identify this oversight as an early critical issue during one.
